name: 王可
objective:
當代英美流行小說, 例如: 帶珍珠耳環的少女, 時空旅人之妻, 姊姊的守護者, 暮光之城系列等等, 主題推陳出新, 內容扣人心弦, 有的反應當前的文化議題, 有的表現出創新的文學想像, 在在都激發著同學們閱讀原文小說的興趣. 又由於小說的書寫語言為當今英語世界所使用, 沒有年代隔閡, 所以原文流行小說也是優良的英語學習材料. 在字彙, 片語, 句型, 段落及文章結構, 到故事情節發展與深入探討主題的每個層面上, 都提供了豐富的素材, 供同學們學習觀摩. 因此, 本課程將挑選不同類型之時下英美流行小說四本, 每月一本, 規劃進度, 在課堂上進行導讀與討論, 並加強字彙, 句型, 與文章結構上的分析, 幫助同學們在英語書寫, 閱讀技巧, 跨文化了解與思辨能力上, 獲得最大的進步!
Contemporary popular novels originally written in English, such as the Girl with a Pearl Earring, the Time Traveler's Wife, and the Twilight, have a strong appeal to readers worldwide, but non-native English speakers often enjoy these works in translated versions or film adaptations. To encourage our students to read these popular English novels in the original language, the instructor will choose four novels of various subject matters and use them as effective teaching materials in the classroom. The objectives are (1) to enrich students' cultural background knowledge of the English speaking world today, (2) to cultivate students' life-long reading habit of keeping up contemporary materials, and (3) to strengthen their critical thinking as well as language skills, especially reading and writing, through line-by-line close readings in the context and guided discussions on the narrative structures of the whole fiction.

Course learning objectives
By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Articulate how fiction creates pleasure or emotional attachment, using specific textual details.
2. Develop interpretations of fiction supported by specific passages and attention to narrative choices.
3. Contribute to literary discussions by offering evidence-based interpretations, asking questions, and responding to other readers.
4. Explain how genre conventions shape narrative choices and reader expectations.
5. Explain how specific publishing practices and reading communities shape a work’s reception.
6. Analyze how a work of popular fiction engages with contemporary desires, anxieties, or social tensions, using textual and contextual evidence.

scorePolicy:
Assessments and grading

1. Class Notebook Portfolio: 20%
We will frequently be doing classwork in this class notebook Google Doc, including interpretations of a text and reflections on how discussion complicated your thinking. You will be assessed on the thoughtfulness of your interpretations and the development of your ideas across the semester.

2. Participation: 20%
Participation includes both your individual contributions and shared class grades from discussions.

Individual participation (15%): Your individual contributions to our classroom community across the semester include your attendance record, individual effort in group work and discussions, and voluntarily asking or answering questions.

Class discussion (5%): The class will receive a shared grade after formal discussions based on the discussion rubric. Your score for this part will be an average of discussion grades across the semester.

3. Student-Led Genre Showcase: 20%
In a group of 3 or 4, you will introduce the class to one short text or carefully selected excerpt that classmates can read in about 8 minutes and that helps us explore a genre or reading community during our “Genre Festival” unit. Genres may include mystery, horror, science fiction, fantasy, romance, YA, and fanfiction. Your group will lead a 30–40 minute session (including reading time), and each member must facilitate part of the class.

4. Event Fieldnote: 15%
Attend one live literary event between Weeks 2 and 15. Possibilities include a book launch, author or translator conversation, reading, panel, or book-club meeting. Other literary events may be proposed if you can explain their connection to the course.
The event may be in Chinese or another language. An approved livestream is acceptable if you attend while it happens. A bookstore visit or browsing a book fair alone does not fulfill the assignment; attend a specific session involving literary conversation.
Submit a 250–500-word fieldnote in English within one week after the event. Describe how the event presented the book and connect your observations to texts or questions from our course. Give a 1–2 minute informal report-back in class.

5. Publishing Pitch: 25%
Select a work of fiction you care about that we have not studied in class. Imagine that you represent the work as an agent and want an Anglophone publisher to acquire it. Research an appropriate publisher or imprint, write a brief pitch, and deliver a short oral pitch to the class.
Make a case for what the work offers readers, who its readers might be, and why it would be a good fit for this publisher. Support your pitch with specific details from the work. You may choose fiction originally written in any language.

AI use
Follow AI guidelines for different tasks. Classwork and assignments will explain how you may use AI. If there are no guidelines, assume that AI use will negatively impact the evaluation of your work.

Preparing for class
Read each week and come prepared to discuss specific passages. Contribute through observations, questions, and responses to classmates. You may ask for clarification or time to think; use notes or partner rehearsal to prepare a contribution. Give others time to speak and help them develop their ideas.

This is a rigorous course designed for students who are seriously interested in reading and vocally engaging with literature. Each student should give their best effort at contributing to the community of the classroom through coming to class prepared, answering questions, participating in discussions, and doing partner work with peers. Students should expect to read every week and develop thoughtful interpretations based on specific details from the texts.
